title: The algebra of a basis cone is a normal polynomial algebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $G$ an abelian group written additively, and $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ a finite integral basis: every $g\in G$ has a unique expression $g=\sum_{i=1}^r n_i u_i$ with $n_i\in\mathbf Z$. Put $H=\{\sum_i a_i u_i:a_i\in\mathbf N\}\subseteq G$. For $T=H$ or $G$, define $k[T]=\bigoplus_{t\in T}ke^t$ with $e^te^{t'}=e^{t+t'}$, and regard $C=k[H]$ as the subalgebra of $k[G]$ supported on $H$. Define $B_0=k$ and $B_i=B_{i-1}[X_i]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring]. The evaluation homomorphism $\phi:B_r\to C$ that fixes $k$ and sends $X_i$ to $e^{u_i}$ is an isomorphism of $k$-algebras. Its inverse sends $e^{\sum_i a_i u_i}$ to $\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$ and extends $k$-linearly. Both $B_r$ and $C$ are normal domains [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. The case $r=0$, where $G=H=\{0\}$ and $B_0=C=k$, is included.

proof.text: For $a\in\mathbf N^r$ put $h(a)=\sum_i a_i u_i$ and $X^a=\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$. The map $h:\mathbf N^r\to H$ is onto by the definition of $H$, and injective because equality of its values is equality of two integral-coordinate expressions in the given basis. Also $h(0)=0$ and $h(a+b)=h(a)+h(b)$. In particular every $h\in H$ has exactly one nonnegative coordinate tuple. Since $0\in H$ and $h(a)+h(b)=h(a+b)\in H$, extension of a coefficient list by zero outside $H$ respects the unit, sums and convolution products. It injects $k[H]$ into $k[G]$: equality there is coefficientwise equality, hence equality on $H$. Its image is exactly the lists supported on $H$, which is the specified subalgebra $C$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed pp.104--105: group coordinates and free monoid identification; explicit elementary coefficient calculation by Q94.

proof.text: By [def-weil-polynomial-ring], a polynomial in $B_i=B_{i-1}[X_i]$ has a unique finite coefficient list in $B_{i-1}$. Induction on $i$, starting with $B_0=k$, therefore expands every element of $B_r$ uniquely as a finite sum $\sum_{a\in\mathbf N^r}c_aX^a$: at the induction step expand each coefficient and append its $X_i$ exponent. Coefficientwise addition adds the $c_a$, and the defining convolution product gives $X^aX^b=X^{a+b}$ by multiplying the powers in each variable.

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.12 proof, printed pp.104--105: group coordinates and free monoid identification; explicit elementary coefficient calculation by Q94.

proof.text: Define $\phi(\sum_a c_aX^a)=\sum_a c_ae^{h(a)}$ and $\psi(\sum_{h\in H}d_he^h)=\sum_a d_{h(a)}X^a$. These sums are finite, since $h$ is a bijection and both input supports are finite. They preserve sums and scalars; on products each sends the pair of basis terms indexed by $a,b$ to the term indexed by $a+b$, with coefficient $c_ad_b$. Distributing the finite sums proves multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Reindexing shows both composites are identities. For each $i$, the coordinate vector with entry $1$ at $i$ and $0$ elsewhere maps to $u_i$, so $\phi(X_i)=e^{u_i}$; the zero vector shows that $\phi$ fixes $k$. Any $k$-algebra homomorphism with these variable images sends $X^a$ to $e^{h(a)}$ and hence has the displayed formula on every finite coefficient expansion. Thus $\phi$ is exactly the stated evaluation homomorphism, and $\psi(e^{\sum_i a_iu_i})=X^a$ is its stated inverse.

proof.text: A field [def-weil-field] is a domain, since $ab=0$ and $a\ne0$ imply $b=a^{-1}ab=0$. Every fraction $a/b$ with $b\ne0$ already equals $ab^{-1}\in k$, so $B_0=k$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Inductively, if $B_{i-1}$ is a normal domain, [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-normal-domain] applies and makes $B_i=B_{i-1}[X_i]$ a normal domain. Finite induction gives the assertion for $B_r$.

source.place: Tag 030A, lemma-polynomial-domain-normal, lines 8130--8150; finite induction from the field base case.

proof.text: The isomorphism makes $C$ a domain: $1_C\ne0$ because $\psi(1_C)=1_{B_r}\ne0$, and $xy=0$ gives $\psi(x)\psi(y)=0$, hence $x=0$ or $y=0$. Define $\widetilde\psi:\operatorname{Frac}(C)\to\operatorname{Frac}(B_r)$ by $x/y\mapsto\psi(x)/\psi(y)$. Denominators stay nonzero by injectivity of $\psi$. Cross-multiplication proves well-definedness, and the fraction formulas for sums and products show this is a ring homomorphism with inverse $a/b\mapsto\phi(a)/\phi(b)$. If $z\in\operatorname{Frac}(C)$ satisfies $z^n+\sum_{j<n}c_jz^j=0$ with $c_j\in C$, applying $\widetilde\psi$ gives $\widetilde\psi(z)^n+\sum_{j<n}\psi(c_j)\widetilde\psi(z)^j=0$. Normality of $B_r$ gives $\widetilde\psi(z)=b\in B_r$, so the inverse fraction map yields $z=\phi(b)\in C$. This is exactly [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. For $r=0$ the exponent tuple is empty, $G=H=\{0\}$, and both maps are the identity of $k$ under $e^0=1$.
